brandsGenerics.title: Brands vs. generics net sales
brandsGenerics.content:
Viatris reports net sales in two product families: Brands (off-patent originator brands it still markets, e.g. Lipitor, Lyrica, Viagra, EpiPen, plus newer launches) and Generics (unbranded multi-source products).

For Viatris Inc.: both lines have shrunk every year since the 2020 Mylan/Upjohn combination -- generics fell from $7.0bn (FY2021) to $5.1bn (FY2025) on loss-of-exclusivity and price erosion, while brands fell more slowly from $10.8bn to $9.2bn. Brands are now ~64% of net sales versus ~61% at spin-off, so the mix is shifting toward the steadier line even though the total is still declining.

What to watch:

  • Whether new-product launches (the R&D ramp below) stabilise the brands line before generics erosion catches up
  • Divestiture proceeds removing revenue without removing debt

segmentMix.title: Net sales by region
segmentMix.content:
Viatris runs four geographic segments: Developed Markets (US, Europe, Japan, Canada, Australia -- the largest and most brand-weighted), Greater China, JANZ (Japan, Australia, New Zealand generics/complex generics) and Emerging Markets.

For Viatris Inc.: Developed Markets alone has fallen from $10.4bn (FY2021) to $8.5bn (FY2025), the single largest driver of the group decline; the other three segments are smaller and comparatively stable, so a Developed Markets stabilisation is the swing factor for the whole top line.

What to watch:

  • Developed Markets net sales inflecting versus still declining
  • Emerging Markets/Greater China growth offsetting the developed-market base erosion

rdIntensity.title: R&D intensity
rdIntensity.content:
R&D expense as a percentage of net sales -- how much of the top line is being reinvested in the new-product pipeline (complex generics, biosimilars, 505(b)(2) brands) that management is counting on to offset the legacy base's decline.

For Viatris Inc.: R&D intensity has nearly doubled, from 3.8% of revenue in FY2021 to 6.8% in FY2025 and in the trailing quarters -- a rising ratio against falling revenue means the dollar increase is even larger, and the 2026 EWSR restructuring program is funding part of that reallocation.

What to watch:

  • Whether the ramp produces launches that show up in the brands line
  • R&D rising as a % purely because revenue is shrinking, not because spend is growing

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Viatris Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Viatris Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Viatris Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Viatris Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Viatris Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Viatris Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Viatris Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Viatris Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Viatris Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Viatris Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
